# 3. Circuit Breaker: Hystrix Clients

Netflix has created a library called [Hystrix](https://github.com/Netflix/Hystrix) that implements the [circuit breaker pattern](https://martinfowler.com/bliki/CircuitBreaker.html). In a microservice architecture, it is common to have multiple layers of service calls, as shown in the following example:

**Figure 3.1. Microservice Graph**

![Hystrix](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/spring-cloud/spring-cloud-netflix/master/docs/src/main/asciidoc/images/Hystrix.png)

  

A service failure in the lower level of services can cause cascading failure all the way up to the user. When calls to a particular service exceed `circuitBreaker.requestVolumeThreshold` (default: 20 requests) and the failure percentage is greater than `circuitBreaker.errorThresholdPercentage` (default: >50%) in a rolling window defined by `metrics.rollingStats.timeInMilliseconds` (default: 10 seconds), the circuit opens and the call is not made. In cases of error and an open circuit, a fallback can be provided by the developer.

**Figure 3.2. Hystrix fallback prevents cascading failures**

![HystrixFallback](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/spring-cloud/spring-cloud-netflix/master/docs/src/main/asciidoc/images/HystrixFallback.png)

  

Having an open circuit stops cascading failures and allows overwhelmed or failing services time to recover. The fallback can be another Hystrix protected call, static data, or a sensible empty value. Fallbacks may be chained so that the first fallback makes some other business call, which in turn falls back to static data.

## 3.1 How to Include Hystrix

To include Hystrix in your project, use the starter with a group ID of `org.springframework.cloud` and a artifact ID of `spring-cloud-starter-netflix-hystrix`. See the [Spring Cloud Project page](https://projects.spring.io/spring-cloud/) for details on setting up your build system with the current Spring Cloud Release Train.

The following example shows a minimal Eureka server with a Hystrix circuit breaker:

```
@SpringBootApplication @EnableCircuitBreaker public class Application { public static void main(String[] args) { new SpringApplicationBuilder(Application.class).web(true).run(args); } } @Component public class StoreIntegration { @HystrixCommand(fallbackMethod = "defaultStores") public Object getStores(Map parameters) { //do stuff that might fail } public Object defaultStores(Map parameters) { return /* something useful */; } }
```

The `@HystrixCommand` is provided by a Netflix contrib library called [“javanica”](https://github.com/Netflix/Hystrix/tree/master/hystrix-contrib/hystrix-javanica). Spring Cloud automatically wraps Spring beans with that annotation in a proxy that is connected to the Hystrix circuit breaker. The circuit breaker calculates when to open and close the circuit and what to do in case of a failure.

To configure the `@HystrixCommand` you can use the `commandProperties` attribute with a list of `@HystrixProperty` annotations. See [here](https://github.com/Netflix/Hystrix/tree/master/hystrix-contrib/hystrix-javanica#configuration) for more details. See the [Hystrix wiki](https://github.com/Netflix/Hystrix/wiki/Configuration) for details on the properties available.

## 3.2 Propagating the Security Context or Using Spring Scopes

If you want some thread local context to propagate into a `@HystrixCommand`, the default declaration does not work, because it executes the command in a thread pool (in case of timeouts). You can switch Hystrix to use the same thread as the caller through configuration or directly in the annotation, by asking it to use a different “Isolation Strategy”. The following example demonstrates setting the thread in the annotation:

```
@HystrixCommand(fallbackMethod = "stubMyService", commandProperties = { @HystrixProperty(name="execution.isolation.strategy", value="SEMAPHORE") } )
```

The same thing applies if you are using `@SessionScope` or `@RequestScope`. If you encounter a runtime exception that says it cannot find the scoped context, you need to use the same thread.

You also have the option to set the `hystrix.shareSecurityContext` property to `true`. Doing so auto-configures a Hystrix concurrency strategy plugin hook to transfer the `SecurityContext` from your main thread to the one used by the Hystrix command. Hystrix does not let multiple Hystrix concurrency strategy be registered so an extension mechanism is available by declaring your own `HystrixConcurrencyStrategy` as a Spring bean. Spring Cloud looks for your implementation within the Spring context and wrap it inside its own plugin.

## 3.3 Health Indicator

The state of the connected circuit breakers are also exposed in the `/health` endpoint of the calling application, as shown in the following example:

```
{"hystrix"{"openCircuitBreakers"["StoreIntegration::getStoresByLocationLink", "status" "CIRCUIT_OPEN"}, "status" "UP"}
```

## 3.4 Hystrix Metrics Stream

To enable the Hystrix metrics stream, include a dependency on `spring-boot-starter-actuator` and set `management.endpoints.web.exposure.include: hystrix.stream`. Doing so exposes the `/actuator/hystrix.stream` as a management endpoint, as shown in the following example:

```
   
```

This page documents Spring Cloud's Circuit Breaker: Hystrix Clients functionality. It explains that Netflix's Hystrix library implements the circuit breaker pattern for microservice architectures, where multiple layers of service calls can cause cascading failures when lower-level services fail. Hystrix opens a circuit when calls to a service exceed `circuitBreaker.requestVolumeThreshold` (default: 20 requests) and the failure percentage exceeds `circuitBreaker.errorThresholdPercentage` (default: >50%) within a rolling window of `metrics.rollingStats.timeInMilliseconds` (default: 10 seconds). When a circuit opens, calls are stopped, and developers can provide fallbacks (which may be another Hystrix-protected call, static data, or an empty value, and can be chained).

To include Hystrix, add the starter with group ID `org.springframework.cloud` and artifact ID `spring-cloud-starter-netflix-hystrix`. The `@HystrixCommand` annotation (provided by Netflix's "javanica" library) is automatically wrapped by Spring Cloud into a proxy connected to the Hystrix circuit breaker. Configuration is done via `commandProperties` with `@HystrixProperty` annotations.

For propagating security context or Spring scopes (`@SessionScope`/`@RequestScope`), the default thread-pool-based execution won't work; developers can switch to the SEMAPHORE isolation strategy via `execution.isolation.strategy` or set `hystrix.shareSecurityContext` to `true` to transfer the SecurityContext. Since Hystrix only allows one concurrency strategy, a custom `HystrixConcurrencyStrategy` can be declared as a Spring bean.

Circuit breaker state is exposed in the `/health` endpoint (e.g., showing "CIRCLE_OPEN" status). To enable the Hystrix metrics stream, add `spring-boot-starter-actuator` and set `management.endpoints.web.exposure.include: hystrix.stream`, which exposes `/actuator/hystrix.stream`.

Circuit breaker pattern for Python microservices using gRPC: integration approaches, tuning, and performance/operational trade-offs. Research the canonical circuit breaker pattern sources (Michael Nygard's Release It! pattern as the original reference, Martin Fowler's "CircuitBreaker" article on martinfowler.com, and resilience library documentation for pybreaker, circuitbreaker (the pip package), and tenacity — the documented APIs and READMEs on PyPI and GitHub, plus Azure Architecture Center circuit breaker guidance and Netflix/Hystrix-style guidance if relevant). Cover: (1) State machine semantics: closed, open, half-open, transition conditions, failure threshold ratios/counts, success counts needed to close, timeout for transitioning from open to half-open. (2) Python implementation options: pybreaker API (CircuitBreaker, listen calls, failure thresholds, reset timeout, scope/caching circuit breaker instances by service or RPC), circuitbreaker package (CIRCUIT_BREAKER_* environment variables, fail_max, reset_timeout, exclude exceptions), tenacity integration (Retrying with stop_after_attempt, wait_exponential, before_sleep, retry_if_exception_type, and how tenacity can act as a retry wrapper around calls; note tenacity itself is not a circuit breaker but can implement one via custom retry predicates or in combination), and custom implementations based on sliding windows (e.g., time-window failure counting, ring buffers) and why naive counters are problematic. (3) Tuning: choosing failure rate thresholds and sliding window durations under tight SLAs, avoiding flapping under bursty traffic, half-open probe traffic volume (e.g., allowing a small percentage of requests through). (4) Interaction with gRPC specifics: how to classify which gRPC status codes should trip the breaker (UNAVAILABLE, DEADLINE_EXCEEDED vs NOT_FOUND, INVALID_ARGUMENT should not trip), mapping grpc.RpcError / grpc.aio.AioRpcError codes to breaker failure predicates, where the breaker should live (client-side per destination service, per channel, per method), and how breakers interact with gRPC channel connection state and pending request queues (when the channel is idle/transient-failure, whether the breaker short-circuits to fail fast). (5) Performance implications: latency saved by fail-fast rejection when open (short-circuiting), added latency overhead of checking breaker state, memory overhead of sliding windows, behavior under concurrency and race conditions on state transitions, and the risk of cascading rejection storms and client-side trailing Goose effects. (6) Reliability trade-offs: protection against cascading failures, but risk of premature tripping under transient spikes, stale state, and interaction with retries (retries should normally be suppressed or reduced when the breaker is open to avoid hammering). (7) Operational complexity: monitoring (trip counts, failure rates, state transitions, probes), tuning difficulty, and how to implement per-key breakers (per RPC method, per downstream service). (8) Best-fit scenarios: downstream dependency failure containment, protecting a degraded dependency; where breakers are counterproductive (canary rollouts, rapid retry-tolerant calls, low-traffic services with sparse calls where thresholds never trip). Provide concrete Python code snippets and API usage examples for pybreaker and tenacity where authoritative, and cite sources precisely. Prioritize English-language authoritative sources.

--- SOURCE 1: The Circuit Breaker Pattern - DEV Community ---
URL: https://dev.to/bearer/the-circuit-breaker-pattern-5gcl

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article, published on DEV Community on January 21, 2020 (originally posted on the Bearer blog), explains the Circuit Breaker design pattern for building resilient applications that depend on services not under the developer's control, such as third-party APIs.

**Core Concept:** A circuit breaker detects the availability of a service and prevents an application from continuously making failed requests until the issue is resolved. Per Martin Fowler: "You wrap a protected function call in a circuit breaker object, which monitors for failures. Once the failures reach a certain threshold, the circuit breaker trips, and all further calls to the circuit breaker return with an error, without the protected call being made at all."

**Three States of a Circuit:**
- **Closed**: Default "everything is working" state, where requests pass freely through.
- **Open**: Rejects all requests without attempting to send them.
- **Half-Open**: A set number of requests are let through to test the resource's status and determine whether the circuit returns to closed or open.

**Threshold Criteria:** States depend on pre-set thresholds that may include error rates in a given time-frame, latency, traffic, or resource utilization. The right criteria depend on the use case—latency matters for speed-critical APIs, while uptime matters more for user-account APIs. Monitoring solutions (like the Bearer Agent) can help analyze API calls to inform circuit breaker decisions. Many libraries, such as opossum for Node.js, allow configurable threshold metrics.

**Code Example with opossum:** The article demonstrates wrapping an API client method in a circuit breaker with configuration options: a 3-second timeout, a 50% error threshold percentage, and a 5-second reset timeout (transitioning from open to half-open state).

**Reaction to Failures:** Circuit breakers delay retries and prevent unnecessary requests, but their true power comes from reacting to breaker states—libraries like opossum allow running fallback functions or responding to emitted events.

**Recommendation:** The author recommends implementing circuit breakers to build resiliency and graceful degradation, not just for external APIs but also for internal microservices. Most languages have community libraries available. Further reading includes Microsoft's Guide to Circuit Breakers and Martin Fowler's original post.

**Comments discussion:** A reader asked whether queues (which can store requests, handle retries, and bake in asynchronicity) might be a better externalized solution; the author replied that queues are a great approach, and the pattern could also apply to a custom-made queue with a circuit breaker added.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"You wrap a protected function call in a circuit breaker object, which monitors for failures. Once the failures reach a certain threshold, the circuit breaker trips, and all further calls to the circuit breaker return with an error, without the protected call being made at all." - Martin Fowler
</key_excerpts>



--------------------------------------------------------------------------------


--- SOURCE 2: Dev-Journal/circuit-breaker-pattern.md at main · spShashankGit/Dev-Journal · GitHub ---
URL: https://github.com/spShashankGit/Dev-Journal/blob/main/circuit-breaker-pattern.md

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a GitHub document (Dev-Journal repository by spShashankGit) containing developer notes on the Circuit Breaker Pattern, a cloud system design pattern. The pattern was popularized by Michael Nygard in his book "Release It!"

Key content:
- Background: Remote calls differ from local calls and are prone to failure due to network/latency. When one supplier system is called by many clients, this can cause cascading failures across multiple systems.
- Circuit breaker concept: Wrap a protected function call in a circuit breaker object that monitors failures. Once failures reach a threshold, the breaker "trips" (State: Open), and all future calls return errors without contacting the protected system. Having an alert for breaker trips is good practice.
- Self-healing (State: Closed): Program the circuit to call the protected system after a suitable interval, resetting the breaker should it succeed.
- Half-open state: After recovery, a trial call is made which either resets the breaker on success or restarts the timeout on failure.
- Gotchas: Not all failures should trip the circuit (normal failures should be handled by regular logic). Use promises for slow remote calls, placing each call on a different thread, and arrange for the circuit to break when the thread pool is exhausted.
- Tripping the breaker: Simple approach (count-based) or sophisticated approach (frequency of errors, e.g., 50% failure rate, or thresholds like 10 timeouts but 3 connection failures).
- Async calls: Circuit breakers are useful for async communications—put requests on a queue consumed by the supplier; the circuit breaks when the queue fills up.
- Applicability: Even without unreliable services, circuit breakers help reduce resources tied up in likely-fail operations, avoiding client timeout waits and avoiding sending requests to struggling servers.

**Core Concepts:** The pattern (originated in Michael Nygard's "Release It!" and popularized by Martin Fowler) wraps remote service calls in a monitoring object that tracks failures. --- SOURCE 6: Circuit breaker pattern - AWS Prescriptive Guidance ---
URL: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/prescriptive-guidance/latest/cloud-design-patterns/circuit-breaker.html

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This AWS Prescriptive Guidance page describes the Circuit Breaker design pattern, a fault-tolerance mechanism that prevents a caller service (e.g., an order service) from retrying calls to another service (e.g., a payment service) when those calls have previously caused repeated timeouts or failures. The pattern, popularized by Michael Nygard in his book "Release It" (2018), operates like an electrical circuit breaker: it "trips" (opens) when the callee is unavailable, and periodically tests to detect when the callee service becomes functional again, at which point the circuit closes and calls resume.

**Motivation:** When microservices in complex applications communicate via remote procedure calls, outages or high latency in one microservice can cascade and cause application-wide failure. While transient errors can be handled with the "retry with backoff" pattern, repeated retries during prolonged failures (e.g., a down service or database contention) can cause network contention and database thread pool exhaustion, especially when exacerbated by multiple users retrying. The pattern also addresses the "fallacies of distributed computing" (assertions by Peter Deutsch and others at Sun Microsystems), which note that applications written without adequate error handling for network errors can hang indefinitely or suffer performance/cost degradation.

**Applicability:** Use the pattern when (1) a call is most likely going to fail, (2) the callee exhibits high latency causing timeouts, or (3) the caller makes a synchronous call to an unavailable or high-latency service.

**Issues and considerations:** Implementation should be microservice-agnostic and API-driven to prevent code bloat; the callee can update circuit status to CLOSED upon recovery (an extension useful when RTO requires it); multithreaded calls should ensure the first failed call defines the expiration timeout and subsequent calls don't endlessly move it; system administrators should be able to force-open or force-close the circuit by updating the expiration timeout; and proper logging/observability should identify calls that fail while the circuit is open.

**AWS Implementation:** The sample solution uses AWS Step Functions (express workflows) to implement the pattern, with the state machine configuring retry capabilities and decision-based control flow. An Amazon DynamoDB table (CircuitStatus) tracks circuit status, storing currently degraded services with an ExpiryTimeStamp; this can be replaced with an in-memory datastore like Amazon ElastiCache (Redis OSS) for better performance. When a service call begins, the workflow checks the CircuitStatus table: an unexpired record causes immediate failure (FAIL state); otherwise, the ExecuteLambda step calls the target service. Failures trigger exponential backoff retries, and persistent failures insert a record with ExpiryTimeStamp and exit with FAIL. Expired items are deleted via DynamoDB TTL. A complete implementation is available in the GitHub repository (github.com/aws-samples/circuit-breaker-netcore-blog), with a related blog post on using the pattern with AWS Step Functions and DynamoDB.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 10: Circuit Breaker ---
URL: https://martinfowler.com/bliki/CircuitBreaker.html

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article by Martin Fowler (published March 6, 2014) explains the Circuit Breaker pattern, popularized by Michael Nygard in his book "Release It," which prevents catastrophic cascading failures in software systems making remote calls.

**Core Concept:** The circuit breaker wraps a protected function call in an object that monitors failures. Once failures reach a threshold, the circuit "trips" (opens), and all further calls return errors without making the protected call. This prevents resource exhaustion when a supplier becomes unresponsive.

**Three States:** The pattern uses three states:
- **Closed** - normal operation, protected calls are made
- **Open** - calls return an error immediately without invoking the protected call, triggered when failure count reaches a threshold
- **Half-open** - after a reset timeout, the breaker makes a trial call to test if the underlying system has recovered; success resets to closed, failure restarts the timeout

**Ruby Example:** The article includes a simple Ruby implementation with `CircuitBreaker` and `ResetCircuitBreaker` classes, demonstrating configuration of invocation timeout, failure threshold, and monitor alerting.

**Advanced Considerations:**
- Breakers can protect against multiple error types (not all errors should trip the circuit)
- Thread pools with futures/promises help handle slow remote calls; circuits can break when the pool is exhausted
- More sophisticated tripping can be based on failure frequency (e.g., 50% failure rate) or different thresholds for different errors (e.g., 10 for timeouts, 3 for connection failures)
- Also useful for asynchronous communication via queues (circuit breaks when queue fills)
- Monitoring is critical - state changes should be logged, and operations staff should be able to manually trip/reset breakers
- Clients must plan failure responses (e.g., queue credit card authorizations, show stale data)

**Further Reading:** Netflix's tech blog on fault tolerance, Netflix's open-source Hystrix tool, and other implementations in Ruby, Java, Grails, C#, AspectJ, and Scala.
</summary>

PyBreaker is a Python implementation of the Circuit Breaker pattern, based on Michael T. Nygard's book "Release It!" The circuit breaker pattern allows one subsystem to fail without destroying the entire system by wrapping dangerous operations (typically integration points) with a component that can circumvent calls when the system is not healthy.

Features include: configurable list of excluded exceptions (e.g., business exceptions), configurable failure threshold and reset timeout, support for several event listeners per circuit breaker, ability to guard generator functions, functions and properties for monitoring/management, thread-safety, optional Redis backing, and optional support for asynchronous Tornado calls.

Requirements: Python 3.10+. Installation via `pip install pybreaker`. Development installation via git clone and editable install.

Usage: Create a CircuitBreaker instance for each integration point (e.g., `db_breaker = CircuitBreaker(fail_max=5, reset_timeout=60)`), which should live globally across requests. A success threshold can be configured to require multiple successful requests before closing the circuit. Optional Redis backing uses CircuitRedisStorage (with unique namespaces for multiple breakers; do not use decode_responses=True). Event listening is done by subclassing CircuitBreakerListener (before_call, state_change, failure, success methods). Functions can be guarded via decorator syntax, direct `.call()` method, or context manager. By default, after 5 consecutive failures the circuit opens, and all calls fail immediately raising CircuitBreakerError (unless throw_new_error_on_trip=False). SUMMARY:
<summary>
This page documents the circuit breaker feature in the Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI) Python SDK, which is used to prevent retries from overwhelming a service during outages. The SDK uses the third-party `circuitbreaker` Python library.

**Purpose & Mechanism:** A protected function call (a REST call) is wrapped in a circuit breaker object that monitors failures. When failures reach a threshold, the circuit breaker trips and all further calls return an error without making the protected call, protecting the service from being overwhelmed during outages.

**Three Circuit Breaker States:**
- **Closed (initial state):** All requests pass through. Successful requests keep the circuit in this state; failures increment the failure count (reset on success). Reaching the failure threshold trips the circuit to Open.
- **Open:** No network calls are allowed to hit the service for a reset timeout duration, after which the circuit transitions to Half Open.
- **Half Open:** The circuit makes a trial call. Success transitions it back to Closed; failure restarts the reset timeout and returns the circuit to Open.

**Configuring Circuit Breakers:**
- By default, SDK clients do NOT have circuit breakers enabled.
- **Client level:** Each client accepts a `circuit_breaker_strategy` keyword argument (can be `DEFAULT_CIRCUIT_BREAKER_STRATEGY`, `NoCircuitBreakerStrategy`, or a custom `CircuitBreakerStrategy`).
- **Global level:** Users can set `oci.circuit_breaker.GLOBAL_CIRCUIT_BREAKER_STRATEGY` programmatically, which applies to all clients unless overridden per-client. Alternatively, the environment variable `OCI_SDK_DEFAULT_CIRCUITBREAKER_ENABLED` (set to True/False) enables/disables the default strategy globally. This environment variable is read only once during SDK initialization.
- **Precedence (highest to lowest):** client-level strategy, then `GLOBAL_CIRCUIT_BREAKER_STRATEGY`, then `OCI_SDK_DEFAULT_CIRCUITBREAKER_ENABLED`.

**Key caveats:**
- Once a client has been configured with a circuit breaker strategy, it cannot be modified or removed.
- The `DEFAULT_CIRCUIT_BREAKER_STRATEGY` should not be modified, but `GLOBAL_CIRCUIT_BREAKER_STRATEGY` can be.
- Some services have circuit breakers enabled by default (following the default strategy); override as needed. Service client descriptions note whether they have circuit breakers enabled by default.

**Callback Functionality:** Users can pass a `circuit_breaker_callback` function when creating a client to perform custom actions (logging, metrics, etc.) whenever an API call is blocked. This function receives one argument of type `CircuitBreakerError`. A sample example is available on GitHub (oracle/oci-python-sdk, circuit_breaker_example.py).
</summary>

--- SOURCE 11: Circuit Breaker Pattern - Azure Architecture Center | Microsoft Learn ---
URL: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/patterns/circuit-breaker

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This page from the Microsoft Azure Architecture Center (last updated 2025-03-21) documents the Circuit Breaker pattern, a cloud design pattern used to temporarily block access to a remote service or resource after failures reach a threshold, preventing an application from repeatedly retrying operations that are likely to fail.

## Context and Problem
In distributed environments, remote calls can fail due to transient faults (overcommitted resources, slow networks, time-outs) that typically self-correct. However, unanticipated events can cause longer-lasting faults. If a service is busy, failures can cascade—blocked requests hold critical system resources (memory, threads, database connections), potentially exhausting them and failing unrelated system parts.

## Solution
The Circuit Breaker pattern acts as a proxy (state machine) with three states:
- **Closed:** Requests route to the operation; the proxy counts failures. Exceeding a threshold within a time period puts the proxy into the Open state and starts a time-out timer.
- **Open:** Requests fail immediately with an exception returned to the application.
- **Half-Open:** A limited number of requests are allowed through. If successful, the breaker returns to Closed (failure counter reset). If any fail, it reverts to Open and restarts the timer.

The failure counter for the Closed state is time-based and resets periodically to prevent tripping on occasional failures. The success counter in Half-Open records consecutive successes before reverting to Closed. The pattern can be adapted with increasing time-outs, returning default values instead of exceptions, and using AI/machine learning for adaptive threshold adjustment based on real-time traffic patterns.

The page notes a distinction from the Retry pattern: Retry enables retrying operations expected to eventually succeed, while Circuit Breaker prevents operations likely to fail. The two can be combined.

## Problems and Considerations
Key implementation factors include: exception handling, examining exception types, monitoring/observability (with distributed tracing), configuring for likely recovery patterns, testing failed operations via health checks, manual override options, handling concurrency without blocking, resource differentiation (e.g., separate shards), accelerated circuit breaking, multiregion deployments, service mesh circuit breakers, failed request replay, inappropriate external time-outs, and adaptability to different compute environments (serverless to containerized).

## When to Use
**Use when:** preventing cascading failures, intelligent traffic routing for multiregion resilience, protecting against slow dependencies to maintain SLOs, and managing intermittent connectivity problems.

**Not suitable when:** managing local private resources, substituting for business logic exception handling, retry algorithms are already sufficient, reset delays would be unacceptable, in message/event-driven architectures (which use dead letter queues), or when failure recovery is managed at infrastructure/platform level.

## Workload Design
The pattern supports the Azure Well-Architected Framework's Reliability pillar (preventing dependency overload, graceful degradation, self-preservation) and Performance Efficiency pillar (avoiding excessive resource usage during recovery). Related references include RE:03 failure mode analysis, transient faults, RE:07 self-preservation, PE:07, and PE:11.

## Example
The page details a real-world implementation using Azure Cosmos DB's lifetime free tier. During seasonal demand spikes, `429` (too many requests) responses trigger the circuit breaker, causing graceful degradation with default/cached responses while Azure Monitor alerts with dynamic thresholds notify operations teams. Flows are described for Closed state (normal operation), Open state (short-circuited requests with degradation, alerting, and possible throughput scaling after approval), and Half-Open state (trial requests leading to reset or reversion). Components include Azure App Service (hosting the web application), Azure Cosmos DB (data store), and Azure Monitor with alerts.

## Related Resources
The page references the Retry pattern and the Health Endpoint Monitoring pattern for related implementations.
</summary>

"The Circuit Breaker pattern helps prevent an application from repeatedly trying to run an operation that's likely to fail. This pattern enables the application to continue running without waiting for the fault to be fixed or wasting CPU cycles on determining that the fault is persistent."

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is the Microsoft Azure Architecture Center documentation for the "Retry pattern," a cloud design pattern that enables applications to handle transient failures (e.g., momentary network connectivity loss, temporary service unavailability, or timeouts when a service is busy) by transparently retrying failed operations when connecting to a service or network resource.

Key content points:
- **Problem**: Applications communicating with cloud elements experience transient faults that are typically self-correcting; repeating the triggering action after a suitable delay is likely to succeed (e.g., a database implementing a throttling strategy may temporarily reject requests until its workload eases).
- **Solution**: Introduce a retry mechanism; if a request fails after a predefined number of attempts, treat the fault as an exception. Many client libraries and cloud services now have built-in retry mechanisms (e.g., Entity Framework Core provides facilities to retry failed database operations).
- **Three retry strategies**: (1) Cancel - if the failure is non-transient or unlikely to succeed on repeat, cancel and report an exception; (2) Retry immediately - for unusual/rare faults like corrupted network packets; (3) Retry after delay - for commonplace connectivity/busy failures, with delays increased incrementally or exponentially until a maximum number of attempts.
- **Logging guidance**: Log early failures as informational entries, and only log the failure of the final retry attempt as an actual error, to avoid flooding operators with alerts.
- **Issues and considerations**: retry policy should be tuned to business requirements (fail fast for noncritical interactive operations vs. more retries for batch operations); aggressive retry policies can degrade busy services; consider idempotency (retries could execute operations more than once with unintended side effects); adjust delays based on exception type; consider transaction consistency.
- **General guidance**: Test retry code thoroughly against various failure conditions; implement retry logic only with full understanding of the failing operation's context; log all connectivity failures; investigate which faults are long-lasting or terminal (use Circuit Breaker pattern for these).
- **When to use**: Present when the application can experience short-lived transient faults where a repeated request could succeed. NOT useful for long-lasting faults, failures from business logic errors, or as a substitute for addressing scalability issues.
- **Workload design**: Aligns with the Azure Well-Architected Framework's Reliability pillar (RE:07 Self-preservation and RE:07 Transient faults).
- **Examples and next steps**: Refer to the "Implement a retry policy with .NET" guide for an Azure SDK example; consider frameworks like Polly (.NET) or Resilience4j (Java); use the Idempotence pattern when processing commands that change business data (e.g., charging a credit card). For most Azure services, client SDKs include built-in retry logic. The Circuit Breaker pattern is the related resource for longer-lasting failures.
</summary>

<summary>
This is a tutorial from GeeksforGeeks (last updated May 20, 2024) explaining how to implement a basic circuit breaker using Hystrix in a Spring Boot microservices application. The circuit breaker is a design pattern that improves system resilience by preventing cascading failures - it monitors failures and opens the circuit when a threshold is reached, preventing further calls to a failing service and allowing the system to recover.

Key terminologies covered include: Circuit Breaker (monitors service health, interrupts calls after consecutive failures), Command (risky action or service call wrapped with circuit breaker functionality), Fallback (backup mechanism providing default behavior when a command fails), Timeout (maximum execution time before a command is considered failed), Rolling Window (time window for monitoring service health metrics), Isolation (using separate threads, thread pools, or semaphores to prevent one command's failure from affecting others), Metrics (success/failure rates, latency, concurrency data), and Thread Pool (used to execute commands asynchronously with isolation).

The tutorial provides 7 step-by-step instructions:
1. Create a Spring Boot project using Spring Initializr with Spring Web, Spring DevTools, and Lombok dependencies, plus the external dependency `spring-cloud-starter-netflix-hystrix 2.0.0.RELEASE`
2. Configure application.properties with `spring.application.name=circuit-breakers-hystrix` and `server.port=8081`
3. Create a RemoteService interface with a `callService()` method that throws InterruptedException
4. Create RemoteServiceSimulator class implementing RemoteService, annotated with `@HystrixCommand(fallbackMethod = "reliable")` - this randomly throws a RuntimeException or returns "Successfully called service!", with the fallback method returning "Default Response"
5. Create a ServiceController with a `@GetMapping("/service")` endpoint that calls the remote service
6. Add `@EnableHystrix` to the main application class
7. Run the application on port 8081, accessing the endpoint at http://localhost:8081/service

The example demonstrates how Hystrix allows specifying fallback methods to degrade functionality gracefully when a service fails.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 18: Configuration · Netflix/Hystrix Wiki · GitHub ---
URL: https://github.com/netflix/hystrix/wiki/configuration

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This GitHub wiki page documents the configuration system for Netflix's Hystrix, a latency and fault tolerance library for distributed systems. Hystrix uses Archaius for its default property implementation, and properties have four levels of precedence: (1) global default from code, (2) dynamic global default property, (3) instance default from code, and (4) dynamic instance property (highest priority).

The page is organized into three main property categories:

**Command Properties** (configured as `hystrix.command.*HystrixCommandKey*.propertyName`):
- **Execution**: `execution.isolation.strategy` (THREAD is default and recommended for HystrixCommands, SEMAPHORE for HystrixObservableCommands; default THREAD), `execution.isolation.thread.timeoutInMilliseconds` (default 1000), `execution.timeout.enabled` (default true), `execution.isolation.thread.interruptOnTimeout` (default true), `execution.isolation.thread.interruptOnCancel` (default false), `execution.isolation.semaphore.maxConcurrentRequests` (default 10)
- **Fallback**: `fallback.isolation.semaphore.maxConcurrentRequests` (default 10), `fallback.enabled` (default true, since 1.2)
- **Circuit Breaker**: `circuitBreaker.enabled` (default true), `circuitBreaker.requestVolumeThreshold` (default 20), `circuitBreaker.sleepWindowInMilliseconds` (default 5000), `circuitBreaker.errorThresholdPercentage` (default 50), `circuitBreaker.forceOpen` (default false, takes precedence over forceClosed), `circuitBreaker.forceClosed` (default false)
- **Metrics**: `metrics.rollingStats.timeInMilliseconds` (default 10000), `metrics.rollingStats.numBuckets` (default 10, must evenly divide window time), `metrics.rollingPercentile.enabled` (default true), `metrics.rollingPercentile.timeInMilliseconds` (default 60000), `metrics.rollingPercentile.numBuckets` (default 6), `metrics.rollingPercentile.bucketSize` (default 100), `metrics.healthSnapshot.intervalInMilliseconds` (default 500)
- **Request Context**: `requestCache.enabled` (default true), `requestLog.enabled` (default true)

**Collapser Properties** (configured as `hystrix.collapser.*HystrixCollapserKey*.propertyName`): `maxRequestsInBatch` (default Integer.MAX_VALUE), `timerDelayInMilliseconds` (default 10), `requestCache.enabled` (default true)

**Thread Pool Properties** (configured as `hystrix.threadpool.*HystrixThreadPoolKey*.propertyName`): `coreSize` (default 10), `maximumSize` (default 10, added in 1.5.9), `maxQueueSize` (default -1, which uses SynchronousQueue; positive values use LinkedBlockingQueue, only applies at initialization), `queueSizeRejectionThreshold` (default 5, not applicable when maxQueueSize == -1), `keepAliveTimeMinutes` (default 1), `allowMaximumSizeToDivergeFromCoreSize` (default false, added in 1.5.9), `metrics.rollingStats.timeInMilliseconds` (default 10000), `metrics.rollingStats.numBuckets` (default 10)

Notable implementation details: As of Hystrix 1.4.12, several metrics-related properties only affect initial metrics creation and changes after startup won't take effect. Thread pool sizing guidance suggests keeping pools as small as possible since they are the primary tool to shed load; a formula for sizing is "requests per second at peak when healthy × 99th percentile latency in seconds + some breathing room." Netflix API runs 100+ commands across 40+ thread pools, with most thread pools set at 10 threads.
</summary>

URL: https://github.com/Netflix/Hystrix/wiki/Metrics-and-Monitoring

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is the GitHub wiki page for Netflix's Hystrix project, documenting its Metrics and Monitoring capabilities. The page explains that as HystrixCommands and HystrixObservableCommands execute, they generate metrics on execution outcomes and latency, available per command key at fine granularities (on the order of seconds). These metrics are useful individually (for debugging) and in aggregate (for alerting/reporting).

The page documents the complete set of Hystrix event types (corresponding to enum com.netflix.hystrix.HystrixEventType), shared between HystrixCommand and HystrixObservableCommand. Key tables include:

- Command Execution Event Types: EMIT, SUCCESS, FAILURE, TIMEOUT, BAD_REQUEST, SHORT_CIRCUITED, THREAD_POOL_REJECTED, SEMAPHORE_REJECTED (with which ones trigger fallback)
- Command Fallback Event Types: FALLBACK_EMIT, FALLBACK_SUCCESS, FALLBACK_FAILURE, FALLBACK_REJECTION, FALLBACK_MISSING
- Other Command Event Types: EXCEPTION_THROWN, RESPONSE_FROM_CACHE, COLLAPSED
- Thread Pool Event Types: EXECUTED, REJECTED
- Collapser Event Types: BATCH_EXECUTED, ADDED_TO_BATCH, RESPONSE_FROM_CACHE

Metrics storage approaches are detailed:
- Up to 1.4.x: Metrics were written to in-memory aggregating data structures. HystrixRollingNumber captures counts of events, and HystrixRollingPercentile captures observations of distributions (e.g., latency, collapser batch size). These support a rolling model using configurable number of buckets (n) and overall window (w). One limitation was the inability to do faceting (e.g., by geographic region).
- 1.5.x and beyond: Metrics were redesigned as first-class streams using RxJava. Each HystrixCommandKey, HystrixThreadPoolKey, and HystrixCollapserKey has event streams (start and completion) that can be subscribed to. Events are emitted into thread-local rx.Subjects. Streams are exposed via observe() methods on classes like HystrixCommandStartStream, HystrixCommandCompletionStream, HystrixThreadPoolStartStream, HystrixThreadPoolCompletionStream, HystrixCollapserEventStream, and HystrixRequestEventsStream. Provided metrics consumers include Bucketed Event Counters, Bucketed Max-Concurrency Counters, and Bucketed Distributions.

The page also documents newer 1.5.0 sample streams: Configuration stream (HystrixConfigurationStream), Utilization stream (sampling semaphore and threadpool utilization), and Request streams (HystrixRequestEventsStream). Examples of SSE stream JSON output for the hystrix-examples-webapp are provided.

Metrics publishers can be implemented via HystrixMetricsPublisher and registered via HystrixPlugins.registerMetricsPublisher(). Included hystrix-contrib implementations are hystrix-servo-metrics-publisher (Netflix Servo) and hystrix-yammer-metrics-publisher (Yammer Metrics). The page details the specific Command Metrics (including informational/status, cumulative and rolling event counts, latency percentiles for run() execution and end-to-end execution, and property values) and ThreadPool Metrics (informational/status, rolling counts, cumulative counts, threadpool state, and property values) published by these implementations.
</summary>

"As HystrixCommands and HystrixObservableCommands execute, they generate metrics on execution outcomes and latency. These are very useful to operators of the system, as they give a great deal of insight into how the system is behaving."

--- SOURCE 20: 3. Circuit Breaker: Hystrix Clients ---
URL: https://cloud.spring.io/spring-cloud-netflix/multi/multi__circuit_breaker_hystrix_clients.html

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This page documents Spring Cloud's Circuit Breaker: Hystrix Clients functionality. It explains that Netflix's Hystrix library implements the circuit breaker pattern for microservice architectures, where multiple layers of service calls can cause cascading failures when lower-level services fail. Hystrix opens a circuit when calls to a service exceed `circuitBreaker.requestVolumeThreshold` (default: 20 requests) and the failure percentage exceeds `circuitBreaker.errorThresholdPercentage` (default: >50%) within a rolling window of `metrics.rollingStats.timeInMilliseconds` (default: 10 seconds). When a circuit opens, calls are stopped, and developers can provide fallbacks (which may be another Hystrix-protected call, static data, or an empty value, and can be chained).

To include Hystrix, add the starter with group ID `org.springframework.cloud` and artifact ID `spring-cloud-starter-netflix-hystrix`. The `@HystrixCommand` annotation (provided by Netflix's "javanica" library) is automatically wrapped by Spring Cloud into a proxy connected to the Hystrix circuit breaker. Configuration is done via `commandProperties` with `@HystrixProperty` annotations.

For propagating security context or Spring scopes (`@SessionScope`/`@RequestScope`), the default thread-pool-based execution won't work; developers can switch to the SEMAPHORE isolation strategy via `execution.isolation.strategy` or set `hystrix.shareSecurityContext` to `true` to transfer the SecurityContext. Since Hystrix only allows one concurrency strategy, a custom `HystrixConcurrencyStrategy` can be declared as a Spring bean.

Circuit breaker state is exposed in the `/health` endpoint (e.g., showing "CIRCLE_OPEN" status). To enable the Hystrix metrics stream, add `spring-boot-starter-actuator` and set `management.endpoints.web.exposure.include: hystrix.stream`, which exposes `/actuator/hystrix.stream`.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"In a microservice architecture, it is common to have multiple layers of service calls... A service failure in the lower level of services can cause cascading failure all the way up to the user."
</key_excerpts>

- Tenets of SRE: ensuring durable focus on engineering, moving fast without breaking SLOs (service level objectives), monitoring, emergency response, change management, demand forecasting/capacity planning, provisioning, efficiency and performance
- Chapter 3 covers embracing risk, measuring service risk, risk tolerance, and error budgets
- Chapter 4 covers service level objectives (SLOs)
- Chapter 5 covers eliminating toil (with the quote: "If a human operator needs to touch your system during normal operations, you have a bug")
- Chapters on monitoring distributed systems, automation, release engineering, simplicity, being on-call, effective troubleshooting, emergency response, incident management, postmortem culture, tracking outages, testing for reliability, software engineering in SRE, load balancing (frontend and datacenter), handling overload, cascading failures, distributed consensus (Paxos), distributed cron, data processing pipelines, data integrity, and reliable product launches

Dan Luu's personal asides and critiques include: skepticism about how SREs truly circumvent the dev/ops split, questions about how to transition from blameful to blameless postmortem cultures, concerns about error budget consumption (with Jessica Kerr's pushback that luck could wipe out a decade of error budget), praise for using deadlines instead of timeouts to prevent cascading failures and zombie requests, and notes on Heroku's response to Rap Genius about random routing simplicity.

Luu concludes by noting this is the most valuable technical book he's read in the past year, though he notes the book's downsides: it's a collection of chapters by different authors with varying quality and significant redundancy. He estimates his notes cover about 20% of the book's content. He also notes this set of notes is an experiment in posting his reading notes online, inspired by Jamie Brandon's notes.

# Embedding an SRE to Recover from Operational Overload

Written by Randall Bosetti  
Edited by Diane Bates

It's standard policy for Google's SRE teams to evenly split their time between projects and reactive ops work. In practice, this balance can be upset for months at a time by an increase in the daily ticket volume. A burdensome amount of ops work is especially dangerous because the SRE team might burn out or be unable to make progress on project work. When a team must allocate a disproportionate amount of time to resolving tickets at the cost of spending time improving the service, scalability and reliability suffer.

One way to relieve this burden is to temporarily transfer an SRE into the overloaded team. Once embedded in a team, the SRE focuses on improving the team's practices instead of simply helping the team empty the ticket queue. The SRE observes the team's daily routine and makes recommendations to improve their practices. This consultation gives the team a fresh perspective on its routines that team members can't provide for themselves.

When you are using this approach, it isn't necessary to transfer more than one engineer. Two SREs don't necessarily produce better results and may actually cause problems if the team reacts defensively.

If you are starting your first SRE team, the approach outlined in this chapter will help you to avoid turning into an operation team solely focused on a ticket rotation. If you decide to embed yourself or one of your reports in a team, take time to review SRE practices and philosophy in [Ben Treynor Sloss's introduction](/sre-book/introduction/) and the material on monitoring in [Monitoring Distributed Systems](/sre-book/monitoring-distributed-systems/).

The following sections provide guidance to the SRE who will be embedded on a team.

## Phase 1: Learn the Service and Get Context

Your job while embedded with the team is to articulate why processes and habits contribute to, or detract from, the service's scalability. Remind the team that more tickets should not require more SREs: the goal of the SRE model is to only introduce more humans as more complexity is added to the system. Instead, try to draw attention to how healthy work habits reduce the time spent on tickets. Doing so is as important as pointing out missed opportunities for automation or simplification of the service.

Teams sliding into ops mode might be convinced that scale doesn't matter for them ("my service is tiny"). Shadow an on-call session to determine whether the assessment is true, because the element of scale affects your strategy.

If the primary service is important to the business but actually is tiny (entailing few resources or low complexity), put more focus on ways in which the team's current approach prevents them from improving the service's reliability. Remember that your job is to make the service work, not to shield the development team from alerts.

On the other hand, if the service is just getting started, focus on ways to prepare the team for explosive growth. A 100 request/second service can turn into a 10k request/second service in a year.

## Identify the Largest Sources of Stress

SRE teams sometimes fall into ops mode because they focus on how to quickly address emergencies instead of how to reduce the number of emergencies. A default to ops mode usually happens in response to an overwhelming pressure, real *or imagined*. After you've learned enough about the service to ask hard questions about its design and deployment, spend some time prioritizing various service outages according to their impact on the team's stress levels. Keep in mind that, due to the team's perspective and history, some very small problems or outages may produce an inordinate amount of stress.

## Identify Kindling

Once you [identify a team's largest existing problems](../../workbook/overload/), move on to emergencies waiting to happen. Sometimes impending emergencies come in the form of a new subsystem that isn't designed to be self-managing. Other sources include:

Knowledge gaps
:   In large teams, people can overspecialize without immediate consequence. When a person specializes, they run the risk of either not having the broad knowledge they need to perform on-call support or allowing team members to ignore the critical pieces of the system that they own.

Services developed by SRE that are quietly increasing in importance
:   These services often don't get the same careful attention as new feature launches because they're smaller in scale and implicitly endorsed by at least one SRE.

Strong dependence on "the next big thing"
:   People might ignore problems for months at a time because they believe the new solution that's on the horizon obviates temporary fixes.

Common alerts that aren't diagnosed by either the dev team or SREs
:   Such alerts are frequently triaged as *transient*, but still distract your teammates from fixing real problems. Either investigate such alerts fully, or fix the alerting rules.

Any service that is both the subject of complaints from your clients and lacks a formal SLI/SLO/SLA
:   See [Service Level Objectives](/sre-book/service-level-objectives/) for a discussion of SLIs, SLOs, and SLAs.

Any service with a capacity plan that is effectively "Add more servers: our servers were running out of memory last night"
:   Capacity plans should be sufficiently forward-looking. If your system model predicts that servers need 2 GB, a loadtest that passes in the short term (revealing 1.99 GB in its last run) doesn't necessarily mean that your system capacity is in adequate shape.

Postmortems that only have action items for rolling back the specific changes that caused an outage
:   For example, "Change the streaming timeout back to 60 seconds," instead of "Figure out why it sometimes takes 60 seconds to fetch the first megabyte of our promo videos."

Any serving-critical component for which the existing SREs respond to questions by saying, "We don't know anything about that; the devs own it"
:   To give acceptable on-call support for a component, you should at least know the consequences when it breaks and the urgency needed to fix problems.

# Phase 2: Sharing Context

After scoping the dynamics and pain points of the team, lay the groundwork for improvement through best practices like postmortems and by identifying sources of toil and how to best address them.

## Write a Good Postmortem for the Team

Postmortems offer much insight into a team's collective reasoning. Postmortems conducted by unhealthy teams are often ineffectual. Some team members might consider postmortems punitive, or even useless. While you might be tempted to review the postmortem archives and leave comments for improvement, doing so doesn't help the team. Instead, the exercise might put the team on the defensive.

Instead of trying to correct previous mistakes, take ownership of the next postmortem. There *will* be an outage while you're embedded. If you aren't the person on-call, team up with the on-call SRE to write a great, blameless postmortem. This document is an opportunity to demonstrate how a shift toward the SRE model benefits the team by making bug fixes more permanent. More permanent bug fixes reduce the impact of outages on team members' time.

As mentioned, you might encounter responses such as "Why me?" This response is especially likely when a team believes that the postmortem process is retaliatory. This attitude comes from subscribing to the Bad Apple Theory: the system is working fine, and if we get rid of all the bad apples and their mistakes, the system will continue to be fine. The Bad Apple Theory is demonstrably false, as shown by evidence [[Dek14]](/sre-book/bibliography#Dek14) from several disciplines, including airline safety. You should point out this falsity. The most effective phrasing for a postmortem is to say, "Mistakes are inevitable in any system with multiple subtle interactions. You were on-call, and I trust you to make the right decisions with the right information. I'd like you to write down what you were thinking at each point in time, so that we can find out where the system misled you, and where the cognitive demands were too high."

## Sort Fires According to Type

There are two types of fires in this simplified-for-convenience model:

* Some fires shouldn't exist. They cause what is commonly called ops work or toil (see [Eliminating Toil](/sre-book/eliminating-toil/)).
* Other fires that cause stress and/or furious typing are actually part of the job.

In either case, the team needs to build tools to control the burn.

Sort the team fires into toil and not-toil. When you're finished, present the list to the team and clearly explain why each fire is either work that should be automated or acceptable overhead for running the service.

# Phase 3: Driving Change

Team health is a process. As such, it's not something that you can solve with heroic effort. To ensure that the team can self-regulate, you can help them build a good mental model for an ideal SRE engagement.

###### Note

Humans are pretty good at homeostasis, so *focus on creating (or restoring) the right initial conditions and teaching the small set of principles needed to make healthy choices*.

## Start with the Basics

Teams struggling with the distinction between the SRE and traditional ops model are generally unable to articulate *why* certain aspects of the team's code, processes, or culture bother them. Rather than trying to address each of these issues point-by-point, work forward from the principles outlined in Chapters [Introduction](/sre-book/introduction/) and [Monitoring Distributed Systems](/sre-book/monitoring-distributed-systems/).

Your first goal for the team should be writing a service level objective (SLO), if one doesn't already exist. The SLO is important because it provides a quantitative measure of the impact of outages, in addition to how important a process change could be. An SLO is probably the single most important lever for moving a team from reactive ops work to a healthy, long-term SRE focus. If this agreement is missing, no other advice in this chapter will be helpful. *If you find yourself on a team without SLOs, first read [Service Level Objectives](/sre-book/service-level-objectives/), then get the tech leads and management in a room and start arbitrating.*

## Get Help Clearing Kindling

You may have a strong urge to simply fix the issues you identify. Please resist the urge to fix these issues yourself, because doing so bolsters the idea that "making changes is for other people." Instead, take the following steps:

1. Find useful work that can be accomplished by one team member.
2. Clearly explain how this work addresses an issue from the postmortem *in a permanent way*. Even otherwise healthy teams can produce shortsighted action items.
3. Serve as the reviewer for the code changes and document revisions.
4. Repeat for two or three issues.

When you identify an additional issue, put it in a bug report or a doc for the team to consult. Doing so serves the dual purposes of distributing information and encouraging team members to write docs (which are often the first victim of deadline pressure). Always explain your reasoning, and emphasize that good documentation ensures that the team doesn't repeat old mistakes in a slightly new context.

## Explain Your Reasoning

As the team recovers its momentum and grasps the basics of your suggested changes, move on to tackle the quotidian decisions that originally led to [ops overload.](https://sre.google/sre-book/dealing-with-interrupts/) Prepare for this undertaking to be challenged. If you're lucky, the challenge will be along the lines of, "Explain why. Right now. In the middle of the weekly production meeting."

If you're unlucky, no one demands an explanation. Sidestep this problem entirely by simply explaining all of your decisions, whether or not someone requests an explanation. Refer to the basics that underscore your suggestions. Doing so helps build the team's mental model. *After you leave, the team should be able to predict what your comment on a design or changelist would be.* If you don't explain your reasoning, or do so poorly, there is a risk that the team will simply emulate that lackadaisical behavior, so be explicit.

Examples of a thorough explanation of your decision:

* "I'm not pushing back on the latest release because the tests are bad. I'm pushing back because the error budget we set for releases is exhausted."
* "Releases need to be rollback-safe because our SLO is tight. Meeting that SLO requires that the mean time to recovery is small, so in-depth diagnosis before a rollback is not realistic."

Examples of an insufficient explanation of your decision:

* "I don't think having every server generate its routing config is safe, because we can't see it."

This decision is probably correct, but the reasoning is poor (or poorly explained). The team can't read your mind, so they very likely might emulate the observed poor reasoning. Instead, try "[…] isn't safe because a bug in that code can cause a correlated failure across the service and the additional code is a source of bugs that might slow down a rollback."

* "The automation should give up if it encounters a conflicting deployment."

Like the previous example, this explanation is probably correct, but insufficient. Instead, try "[…] because we're making the simplifying assumption that all changes pass through the automation, and something has clearly violated that rule. If this happens often, we should identify and remove sources of unorganized change."

## Ask Leading Questions

Leading questions are not loaded questions. When talking with the SRE team, try to ask questions in a way that encourages people to think about the basic principles. It's particularly valuable for *you* to model this behavior because, by definition, a team in ops mode rejects this sort of reasoning from its own constituents. Once you've spent some time explaining your reasoning for various policy questions, this practice reinforces the team's understanding of SRE philosophy.

Examples of leading questions:

* "I see that the TaskFailures alert fires frequently, but the on-call engineers usually don't do anything to respond to the alert. How does this impact the SLO?"
* "This turnup procedure looks pretty complicated. Do you know why there are so many config files to update when creating a new instance of the service?"

Counterexamples of leading questions:

* "What's up with all of these old, stalled releases?"
* "Why does the Frobnitzer do so many things?"

# Conclusion

Following the tenets outlined in this chapter provides an SRE team with the following:

* A technical, possibly quantitative, perspective on why they should change.
* A strong example of what change looks like.
* A logical explanation for much of the "folk wisdom" used by SRE.
* The core principles needed to address novel situations in a scalable manner.

Your final task is to write an after-action report. This report should reiterate your perspective, examples, and explanation. It should also provide some action items for the team to ensure they exercise what you've taught them. You can organize the report as a postvitam,[145](#id-p8BuzSWtjs2) explaining the critical decisions at each step that led to success.

The bulk of the engagement is now complete. Once your embedded assignment concludes, you should remain available for design and code reviews. Keep an eye on the team for the next few months to confirm that they're slowly improving their capacity planning, emergency response, and rollout processes.

# Addressing Cascading Failures

Written by Mike Ulrich

> If at first you don't succeed, back off exponentially.
>
> Dan Sandler, Google Software Engineer

> Why do people always forget that you need to add a little jitter?
>
> Ade Oshineye, Google Developer Advocate

A cascading failure is a failure that grows over time as a result of positive feedback.[107](#id-GbduZFnh9) It can occur when a portion of an overall system fails, increasing the probability that other portions of the system fail. For example, a single replica for a service can fail due to overload, increasing load on remaining replicas and increasing their probability of failing, causing a domino effect that takes down all the replicas for a service.

We’ll use the Shakespeare search service discussed in [Shakespeare: A Sample Service](/sre-book/production-environment#xref_production-environment_shakespeare) as an example throughout this chapter. Its production configuration might look something like [Figure 22-1](#fig_cascading-failure_basic-architecture).
